thesis: This episode argues that TSMC is currently 'on top' following Morris Chang's return and a significant payoff from a 'bet-the-farm' deal with Apple. It contrasts this dominance with the historical underestimation of Apple's in-house chip design and notes that while companies like Google and Intel face challenges, the semiconductor landscape is defined by major players like NVIDIA, Samsung, and MediaTek.

claims.claim: The speaker describes TSMC's situation as 'awesome' and notes that the company is 'on top' after Morris Chang's return and subsequent leadership.
claims.quote: David: Totally. But still, great for TSMC. It's awesome. 2005, Morris is 74 years old. He's like, all right, I did it. I've been buying TSMC stock with my own money. It's done well enough.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights that TSMC had a 'bet-the-farm deal' with Apple that paid off significantly, speaking to founder gravitas.
claims.quote: Ben: $9 billion of manufacturing capacity just for a deal with one company, it paid off. David: That was a bet-the-farm deal and something only Morris could do.

claims.claim: The speaker states that TSMC is 'on top' after the company's strategic moves and leadership transitions.
claims.quote: David: Even if he had no equity as a founder, no equity that he didn't buy. After getting that deal done in 2013, Morris stepped down as CEO again, but he stays on as chairman. Then finally, once it all plays out and TSMC is on top, in June of 2018, Morris retires presumably for real.

claims.claim: The speaker questions why NVIDIA has such a large market cap, implying it is due to factors beyond just the PlayStation contract.
claims.quote: David: Why is NVIDIA now a $300–$400 billion market cap company? It's not because of the PlayStation.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that NVIDIA's market cap is twice that of Intel's.
claims.quote: Ben: It's bigger than Intel, right? NVIDIA is 2x Intel's market cap, something like that.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Apple is competing head-to-head with Samsung and has been designing its own chip architecture in-house.
claims.quote: Ben: It was Apple basically saying, we think a lot of people are going to buy a lot of iPhones in the future, and we are competing head-to-head with Samsung because they're a company that is not clear on strategy. They have a consumer angle here with the Galaxy phones. They think they're also kind of a foundry.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Rick Tsai is now the CEO of MediaTek, which spun out of TSMC.
claims.quote: David: Rick is CEO of MediaTek, which spun out of TSMC. He's doing fine. Rick's doing great, but Morris comes back.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Google had no notion of how big smartphones were about to become.
claims.quote: Ben: We should say, 2009 was an interesting tipping point because if you'll remember back to the 2007 introduction to the iPhone, Steve Jobs has a slide where he says their hope, their goal is to get 1% of the existing smartphone market. Google had no notion of how big smartphones were about to become.

claims.claim: The speaker clarifies that Tesla uses Samsung for some of its chips, and possibly fabs them in Austin in the US.
claims.quote: Ben: When we should say we should clarify too, I think Tesla uses Samsung. David: Interesting. I didn't know that. Ben: Not TSMC, or at least for part of it. I think they actually even fab their chips in Austin in the US.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Samsung is both a chip designer and a manufacturer.
claims.quote: Ben: We should say, Samsung also fabbed it because Samsung is both chip designer and a manufacturer.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the majority of cloud workloads are still on CPUs today.
claims.quote: Ben: The majority of cloud workloads are still on CPUs today.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Apple was relying on TSMC, which was then seen as an also-ran.
claims.quote: Ben: No. But Bloomberg reported that it was a really big risk for both companies, both Apple and TSMC. Apple was relying on a company that was then seen as an also-ran.

numbers.what: gross margins of TSMC
numbers.quote: Because they have 50% gross margins and 40% operating margins, they can take that profit and apply more advanced machinery to build more fabs.

numbers.what: operating margins of TSMC
numbers.quote: Because they have 50% gross margins and 40% operating margins, they can take that profit and apply more advanced machinery to build more fabs.

numbers.what: number of companies at leading edge in early 2000s
numbers.quote: In the early 2000s, when TSMC finally caught up to the leading edge level of technology with other semiconductor companies, there were 22 companies that were at the leading edge.

numbers.what: number of companies at leading edge by late 2000s
numbers.quote: By the late 2000s, it had gone from 22 down to 14 that were at the leading edge.

numbers.what: number of companies at leading edge by mid-2010s
numbers.quote: By the mid-2010s, there were six.

numbers.what: number of companies at 5-nanometer process
numbers.quote: Today, there are two at 5-nanometer process is the current leading edge.

numbers.what: process size for next launch by TSMC
numbers.quote: The next process is going to be 3 nanometers. TSMC is going to launch that next year.

numbers.what: Intel's investment in EUV lithography
numbers.quote: Intel was the biggest early investor in EUV committing more than $4 billion to it in 2012.

numbers.what: TSMC's stock price relative to Intel
numbers.quote: I think TSMC is 2.5x Intel stock price.

numbers.what: Intel's market share in computer processors
numbers.quote: They still control 80% of the computer processor market

numbers.quote: if something is going to be true 10% of the time and fail 90% of the time

numbers.what: yield of IBM's own plant for transistors
numbers.quote: IBM's own plant is churning out transistors with about a 10% yield. Which means that of every 100 chips that they churn out of the plant, 90% of them fail and only 10% of them work.

numbers.what: yield of TI's line when Morris shows up
numbers.quote: The TI line has about a 0% yield. They're lucky if they're getting any. Almost everything coming off the line fails at TI when Morris shows up.

numbers.what: yield Morris achieved at the TI plant after four months
numbers.quote: He starts doing some stuff and after about four months, he gets the yields at the TI plant up to 20%. Twice as good as the first party line at IBM.

numbers.what: duration of Morris's PhD at Stanford
numbers.quote: He finished his PhD in 2½ years. Wild.

numbers.what: year Morris became general manager of a semiconductor division at TI
numbers.quote: In 1967, TI made him a general manager of one of the divisions within the semiconductor business, and that's where he had his next big breakthrough.

numbers.what: operating margins of TSMC as a contract manufacturer
numbers.quote: TSMC has 40% operating margins as a contract manufacturer.
